sections.body_en:
There are four levels of supernal revelation: 1) prophecy (above, chapter 16); 2) ruaḥ ha-kodesh (divine inspiration, literally "the holy spirit"), which has many branches (below, sections 4-8); 3) the Urim Ve-tumim, which are one of the branches of ruaḥ ha-kodesh; 4) the bat kol (heavenly voice).

Both in prophecy and in the high levels of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, the divine revelation is received clearly, without doubt or error, above and beyond what a person ordinarily grasps in the usual way through his intellect. However, the level of prophecy is higher than ruaḥ ha-kodesh, for the light of prophecy is brighter and stronger, and through it the cleaving to God is greater and the revelation is more certain and more tangible, similar to something a person sees and feels with his senses (Derekh Hashem, part 3, 3:1-4). Even when the divine revelation came in a dream, it was clear to the prophet whether it was a divine revelation at the level of prophecy or at the level of ruaḥ ha-kodesh (Guide for the Perplexed 2:45).

When the prophet receives prophecy, all his thoughts, emotions and sensations are nullified, and out of tremendous cleaving to the Source of all life he becomes a vessel for receiving the prophecy. However, when receiving ruaḥ ha-kodesh, the person remains with his thoughts, emotions and sensations, and in this manner he merits divine revelation. An example is King David, who composed the psalms of Tehillim and led Israel with the help of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, as it is stated (II Shmuel 23:1-3): "Now these are the last words of David: The saying of David the son of Yishai, and the saying of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Yaakov, and the sweet singer of Israel. The spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and His word was upon my tongue. The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: [Be] a ruler over men, a righteous one, ruling in the fear of God."

Since there are two levels, there is a division in the Tanakh between the section of the 'Prophets' (Nevi'im), the books of which were written through prophecy, and the 'Writings' (Ketuvim), which were written through ruaḥ ha-kodesh. Even prophets who merited to receive revelations through prophecy sometimes merited revelations through ruaḥ ha-kodesh. For example, Shmuel the prophet wrote the book of Shoftim and the book of Shmuel through prophecy, and therefore they are included in the 'Prophets', whereas he wrote Megillat Rut through ruaḥ ha-kodesh, and therefore it is in the 'Writings'. Likewise, Yirmeyahu wrote his own book and the book of Melakhim through prophecy, and wrote Megillat Eikha through ruaḥ ha-kodesh. Similarly, it stands to reason that when prophets answered personal questions, they availed themselves of ruaḥ ha-kodesh (see Guide for the Perplexed 2:45; Rabbeinu Baḥya, Vayikra 8:8; Radak, introduction to Tehillim; Or Hashem, ma'amar 2, 4:2; Abarbanel, Shemot 15).

Although the level of prophecy is higher, in a certain respect ruaḥ ha-kodesh has an advantage over prophecy, because its light spreads through wisdom and grants a broader and more comprehensive understanding. In this respect the stature of Daniel, who was not a prophet but merited ruaḥ ha-kodesh, was higher than the stature of the prophets Ḥaggai, Zekharya and Malakhi, who did not see the great picture concerning the future of the world and the clashes of the kingdoms (Megilla 3a). Similarly, they said: "A sage is preferable to a prophet" (as explained below, section 7).1

notes_en.en:
Rabbeinu Baḥya (Devarim 33:8) divided the revelations into the four levels that I cited at the beginning of this halakha. In prophecy the thoughts and emotions are nullified, and in ruaḥ ha-kodesh they are not nullified; so wrote the Radak and the Meiri in their introductions to Tehillim; Rabbeinu Baḥya, Vayikra 8:8; Devarim 33:8; Abarbanel, Shemot 15. So too wrote the Guide for the Perplexed 2:45 (regarding the second level), and going further, the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 7:2) regarding prophecy that at the time of receiving it a person loses his composure [lit. "his faculties"], and the Ran and the Meiri cited his words. But many disagreed with the Rambam, because we find many prophets who received prophecy without losing their composure (above 16, note 5). It seems that the dispute concerns the state of the body, but all would agree that at the time of receiving prophecy the prophet's thoughts, emotions and sensations are nullified. In Sefer Ha-akeida (gate 6) he wrote that prophecy derives from the level of the neshama, and ruaḥ ha-kodesh from the level of the ruaḥ, which is lower than the neshama.
After Rabbeinu Baḥya (Devarim 33:8) explained that the level of prophecy is above ruaḥ ha-kodesh, he wrote in the name of the Ramban: "Ruaḥ ha-kodesh is the greatest of them all," for "ruaḥ ha-kodesh is wisdom (ḥokhma), which is a spirit drawn from the holy, which is the supernal source." That is to say, ruaḥ ha-kodesh descends from the sefira of Ḥokhma through Malkhut, whereas prophecy derives from the sefirot of Netzaḥ and Hod, so that the revelation of prophecy is higher, while on the other hand the root of ruaḥ ha-kodesh is higher. Furthermore, ruaḥ ha-kodesh is received in Malkhut, and therefore through it one can understand the Torah in a broader and more comprehensive way. For this reason a sage is preferable to a prophet (Bava Batra 12a). Similar to this was written in the book Ateret Tzvi on the Zohar, Aḥarei Mot 61a. (See further below, halakha 7.)
Our master Rav Kook wrote (Orot Ha-kodesh 2, 94) that prophecy actualizes the faculty of ruaḥ ha-kodesh in a more developed way. And since the basis is ruaḥ ha-kodesh, the level of prophecy is in accordance with the magnitude of the attainment in ruaḥ ha-kodesh. And there are those who merited a high level of ruaḥ ha-kodesh but did not merit prophecy, and then they will be at a level of broader understanding than a prophet; however, in that very matter which the prophet attained, the prophet reached a higher and more developed level. Therefore, as a rule, the 'Prophets' section of the Tanakh is more important than the 'Writings', but sometimes the Writings are more important, and therefore in halakha they are equal, in that it is permitted to place books of the Writings on top of books of the Prophets (Rema, YD 282:19). And sometimes the Writings even precede the Prophets, as in the order of Malkhuyot, Zikhronot and Shofarot of Rosh Hashana. And similarly we find (Megilla 3a) regarding the relationship between Daniel and Ḥaggai, Zekharya and Malakhi: "They are superior to him (they are superior to Daniel) – for they are prophets and he is not a prophet (for they are prophets and their books are in the 'Prophets', and he is not a prophet, and his book is in the 'Writings'). He is superior to them (he is superior to them) – for he saw, and they did not see" (for he saw and they did not see).

sections.body_en:
The Urim Ve-tumim are one of the branches of the revelations of ruaḥ ha-kodesh. The breastplate (ḥoshen) was one of the eight garments of the High Priest, and on it were precious stones bearing the names of the Patriarchs and the twelve tribes, as it is stated (Shemot 28:29): "And Aharon shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goes into the holy place, for a remembrance before the Lord continually." The Torah commanded (ibid. 28:30): "And you shall put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Tumim," which were a writing of the Explicit Name (Shem Ha-meforash) that they placed inside the folds of the breastplate, and through them the letters of the breastplate would light up the answers to questions (Rashi and Ramban there). The role of the Urim Ve-tumim was to reveal the judgment of the children of Israel, that is, guidance pertaining to the whole of Israel, as it is stated (ibid.): "And they shall be upon Aharon's heart when he goes in before the Lord, and Aharon shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his heart before the Lord continually." When the leaders of Israel wished to inquire of God, they would come to the High Priest, and the High Priest would stand with his face toward the Holy, and the inquirer would stand behind him and ask his question in a quiet voice. In response, the letters on the breastplate would light up, and the High Priest, with the help of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, would combine the illuminated letters according to their order into meaningful words, and reply with God's answer (see Rashi and Ramban there; Rambam, Hilkhot Klei Ha-mikdash 10:11). And although the decree of a prophet in the name of God is sometimes reversed, for example when the people repented and the decree was annulled (above 16:14), a decree of the Urim Ve-tumim is not reversed. Therefore they are called Urim Ve-tumim: Urim – for they illuminate their words; Tumim – for they complete (mashlimim) their words to the end (tom) (Yoma 73b).

Moshe Rabbeinu did not need to inquire through the Urim Ve-tumim, because he could ask God at any time (above 16:9); it follows that the Urim Ve-tumim were intended for the leaders who arose after him. As God said to Moshe Rabbeinu when He commanded him to appoint Yehoshua bin Nun as his successor: "And he shall stand before Elazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the Lord; at his word they shall go out and at his word they shall come in, he and all the children of Israel with him, and all the congregation" (Bamidbar 27:21).

Generally the leaders of Israel would inquire of the Urim Ve-tumim before deciding to go out to battle. Also when the Land was divided among the tribes in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, they availed themselves of ruaḥ ha-kodesh and the Urim Ve-tumim (Bava Batra 122a). Sometimes, when there was a grave sin on the part of the king or the people, they did not merit to receive an answer through the Urim Ve-tumim, as happened twice to King Shaul (I Shmuel 14:37; 28:6); or an answer was received that led to defeat in battle, as happened to the people of Israel in the war with Binyamin (Shoftim 20:18, 23).

At the beginning of the days of the Second Temple, after the last prophets had died, the Urim Ve-tumim ceased (Mishna Sota 9:12), and they are one of the five things that were in the First Temple and were not in the Second Temple (Yoma 21b). The Urim Ve-tumim ceased because they depend on ruaḥ ha-kodesh, and with the departure of prophecy, the part of ruaḥ ha-kodesh that resembles prophecy also departed, and consequently the possibility of availing oneself of them ceased.2

notes_en.en: The Ramban (Shemot 28:30) explains that the level of the Urim Ve-tumim is below prophecy and above the bat kol. Examples of inquiring through the Urim Ve-tumim: in Shoftim 1:1-2, Israel asked who would go up first to fight the Canaanites, and God answered: "Yehuda shall go up." When making the covenant with the Giv'onim they did not ask the word of God and they stumbled (Yehoshua 9:14). In the war of Israel against Binyamin they inquired three times (Shoftim 20:18; 23; 27-28). Shmuel's choice of Shaul was with the aid of the Urim Ve-tumim (I Shmuel 10:20-22). In Shaul's war against the Philistines he inquired through the Urim Ve-tumim (ibid. 14:36-42). He also inquired before the war at Gilboa, but God did not answer him (ibid. 28:6). When David fled from Shaul, Evyatar the priest fled with him with the Urim Ve-tumim, and since David was a leader in Israel and destined to reign, he could inquire through the Urim Ve-tumim; and so he asked whether to fight the Philistines and save the people of Ke'ila, and God answered that he should fight (ibid. 23:2), and likewise when fleeing from Shaul (ibid. 23:11-12), and likewise in his war against Amalek (ibid. 30:8). Likewise, after Shaul's death he asked whether to go up to one of the cities of Yehuda, and God answered that he should go up to Ḥevron (II Shmuel 2:1). When the Philistine army came up against him he asked whether to fight, and God answered that he should fight and would prevail (ibid. 5:19; 23). In the days of the famine he asked for what they were being punished, and the answer was: because Shaul had put the Giv'onim to death (ibid. 21:1).

sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Sota 48b): "When the last prophets – Ḥaggai, Zekharya and Malakhi – died, ruaḥ ha-kodesh departed from Israel, but nevertheless they would make use of a bat kol." For example, after Yonatan ben Uziel translated the books of the 'Prophets' according to the tradition of interpretation handed down from the last prophets, Ḥaggai, Zekharya and Malakhi, "a bat kol came forth and said: Who is this who has revealed My secrets to mankind? Yonatan ben Uziel stood up on his feet and said: It is I who have revealed Your secrets to mankind; it is revealed and known before You that I did not do it for my own honor, nor for the honor of my father's house, but I did it for Your honor, so that disputes should not multiply in Israel. He further sought to reveal a translation of the Writings; a bat kol came forth and said to him: Enough!" – because through the translation of the Writings he might reveal the end [time] of the Mashiaḥ. Following this bat kol, he refrained from translating the Writings (Megilla 3a). In the period of the Amora'im, too, rare revelations of a 'bat kol' are still related (see Eruvin 54b; Bava Batra 58a). After that, these revelations ceased entirely (Zohar 1:238a).

A bat kol is a divine revelation that conveys a message, akin to prophecy, and it is called a 'bat kol' (literally, "daughter of a voice") because it is an offshoot of the divine voice that is revealed in prophecy, like the echo that returns from the original voice, for one does not hear the divine voice itself but rather the voice born from it (Tosafot, Sanhedrin 11a). Accordingly, a 'bat kol' is generally not directed at a particular person, but is rather general knowledge, which anyone fit for it perceives. For example, as the Sages said: "Every single day a bat kol goes forth from Mount Ḥorev, proclaiming and saying: Woe to the creatures for the insult to the Torah" (Avot 6:2). "Every single day a bat kol goes forth and says: The daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so, the field of so-and-so to so-and-so" (Mo'ed Katan 18b). Likewise, after King Shlomo instituted eruvin and the washing of the hands, a bat kol went forth agreeing with his words (Shabbat 14b). Sometimes the bat kol was directed at particular people, who alone heard it, such as Nevukhadnetzar, who heard a bat kol calling on him to destroy the Temple (Midrash Tehillim 79:2). Since the bat kol is akin to prophecy, at times it speaks in the name of God. And so it is related of Rabbi Yossi that he entered a ruin and heard a bat kol saying: "Woe to the children, because of whose sins I destroyed My house, burned My sanctuary and exiled them among the nations" (Berakhot 3a).

sections.title_en: Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh after the Departure of Prophecy
sections.body_en:
As we learned in the previous halakha, the Sages said (Sota 48b): "When the last prophets – Ḥaggai, Zekharya and Malakhi – died, ruaḥ ha-kodesh departed from Israel." The Sages explained (Yoma 9b) that prophecy departed at the beginning of the days of the Second Temple, when it became clear that although the possibility of going up to the Land had opened, and despite the words of the last prophets who encouraged the aliya, the settlement and the building of the Temple, the majority of Israel remained in the Babylonian exile. And as we learned (above 16:6), prophecy depends on the Land of Israel, for all the prophets prophesied in the Land of Israel or for its sake, and the holiness of the Land is not properly manifest when the majority of Israel do not dwell in it (see Peninei Halakha: Kashrut 12:2).

However, not all the branches of ruaḥ ha-kodesh ceased with the departure of prophecy, but only the part resembling prophecy, which is the divine revelation that rests upon individuals of Israel by the will of Heaven, and without this, even one who refines himself in the most perfect way will not merit prophecy or this kind of ruaḥ ha-kodesh. Therefore, since the days of the Second Temple, because Israel is in a state that is unfit for prophecy, even the very greatest have not merited prophecy or the ruaḥ ha-kodesh intended for the sake of the whole of Israel. As the Sages related (Sota 48b): "Once they were reclining in the upper chamber of the house of Guriya in Jericho, and a bat kol was given to them from heaven, saying: There is among you one man who is fit for the Shekhina to rest upon him, but his generation is not fit for it. They set their eyes on Hillel the Elder, and when he died they eulogized him: Alas, the pious one! Alas, the humble one! Disciple of Ezra. And again, another time, they were reclining in an upper chamber in Yavne, and a bat kol was given to them from heaven, saying to them: There is among you one man who is fit for the Shekhina to rest upon him, but his generation is not worthy of it. They set their eyes on Shmuel Ha-katan, and when he died they eulogized him: Alas, the humble one! Alas, the pious one! Disciple of Hillel."

But the revelations and inspiration of ruaḥ ha-kodesh that depend on a person's deeds did not cease, and whoever merits to sanctify himself through Torah study, the refinement of his character traits and good deeds, merits ruaḥ ha-kodesh. As is brought in Tanna Devei Eliyahu (Rabba 10): "I call heaven and earth to witness concerning me: whether gentile or Jew, whether man or woman, whether manservant or maidservant – all according to the deed that one does, so does ruaḥ ha-kodesh rest upon him." Therefore, even after the departure of prophecy, there were Sages, such as Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai, who saw things through ruaḥ ha-kodesh (Eruvin 64b; Yerushalmi Shevi'it 9:1; Sota 1:4, and elsewhere).

Likewise, hundreds of years after prophecy and ruaḥ ha-kodesh ceased, Rabbi Pinḥas ben Yair explained (Avoda Zara 20b) the path of ascent in character traits up to the attainment of ruaḥ ha-kodesh: "Torah leads to watchfulness, watchfulness leads to zeal, zeal leads to cleanliness, cleanliness leads to abstinence, abstinence leads to purity, purity leads to piety, piety leads to humility, humility leads to fear of sin, fear of sin leads to holiness, holiness leads to ruaḥ ha-kodesh, and ruaḥ ha-kodesh leads to the resurrection of the dead." Likewise we find in the book Sha'ar Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh that the Arizal composed kavanot and yiḥudim (mystical intentions and unifications) for attaining ruaḥ ha-kodesh, and likewise his disciple Rabbi Ḥayim Vital wrote the book Sha'arei Kedusha, which contains guidance for this.

It follows, then, that when the Sages said that with the death of the last prophets ruaḥ ha-kodesh departed, their intent was to the ruaḥ ha-kodesh that is akin to prophecy, which rests upon a person by the will of Heaven and for the sake of the whole of Israel. But the ruaḥ ha-kodesh that rests upon sages by virtue of their spiritual elevation and their deeds has not ceased.3

notes_en.en: In Beit Shlomo (OḤ 112) he cited sources showing that prophecy was sometimes called ruaḥ ha-kodesh, and explained that what departed at the beginning of the days of the Second Temple was the ruaḥ ha-kodesh that is close to the level of prophecy, but ruaḥ ha-kodesh in general, although it diminished, still remained. This is what the Sages said (Sukka 45b): there is no generation that has fewer than thirty-six righteous people who receive the presence of the Shekhina every day. Similarly wrote the Divrei Ḥayim (YD 2:105); Rav Reuven Margaliot (his introduction to Responsa Min Ha-shamayim, p. 25); Rav Yosef Mashash (Otzar Ha-mikhtavim 1:50). And so wrote the Alei Tamar (Yerushalmi Sota 9:13): "Say, then, that ruaḥ ha-kodesh at the level of the prophets, in vision and revelation, or [where one] heard a voice from the mouth of the Almighty – ceased when the last prophets died. But ruaḥ ha-kodesh at the level of wisdom, in which a wise and pious person is endowed with understanding from on high to grasp the secrets of the Torah and the secrets of the world, which plain intellect does not grasp – this has never ceased." My teacher and master, Rav Tzvi Yehuda, explained that prophecy is principally for Israel, while ruaḥ ha-kodesh is also for gentiles. See above 16:5, note 3, and Peninei Halakha: Giyur 1:6.

sections.title_en: Levels in the Sources of Spiritual Revelations
sections.body_en:
Rabbi Ḥayim Vital explained (Sha'arei Kedusha 3:7) that there are five modes of spiritual revelation after prophecy ceased:

The first: that a supernal light be drawn to his soul from the root of his soul on high, and through this he will merit lofty attainments; this is the usual level of ruaḥ ha-kodesh (ibid. 3:5). However, great caution is needed in this, for one who is not clean of sins – the revelations he receives will also be mixed with good and evil, truth and falsehood.

The second: every person who fulfills a mitzva creates thereby a good angel, that is, a spiritual force that adds blessing to the world and pleads in his favor. As the Mishna says (Avot 4:11): "One who performs one mitzva acquires for himself one advocate, and one who commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser." The more a person merits to cleave to God, to study Torah for its own sake and to beautify his fulfillment of the mitzvot, the greater and holier the angels he merits to create, until he can merit revelations through them, and these are what is called a 'maggid'. But if there is a flaw in his Torah and in the intention of his mitzvot, the maggid that is revealed to him will also be mixed with good and evil, truth and falsehood (more on this in the next halakha).

The third: there are those who, instead of receiving a maggid, merit to receive a revelation of Eliyahu the prophet, and according to the measure of his piety so the revelation grows. Those who merit 'the revelation of Eliyahu' are those who walk in the way of Eliyahu the prophet, who devoted himself, at the risk of his life, to the honor of God and to the whole of Israel (as related in I Melakhim, chapters 18-19).

The fourth: there are those who merit that the soul of a righteous person from among the prophets, or from among the early or later sages, is revealed to them, and this is when they are bound to the root of his soul and walk in his way, for example if they studied according to his method or merited to perform a mitzva properly as he did. Concerning this level Rabbi Ḥayim Vital wrote that it is "the greatest of them all," "and one who merits this level will attain that he [the righteous person] will make known to him wisdom and secrets hidden in the Torah, to a wondrous degree, and all this according to his deeds."4

The fifth: those who merit revelations like the first four, but in a dream, and this level is lower than the first four (on dreams, see below chapter 27. There is a prophetic dream, that is, it becomes known to him through prophecy that this dream is actual prophecy; Guide for the Perplexed 2:45).

The Arizal said that a person may believe that the revelations he received are true if it becomes clear to him, through reliable examination, that everything the maggid said is correct and true and not even one letter of his words failed, and also he knows, by means of the revelation, how to explain the mysteries of the Torah and its secrets, and also the intention of the revelation is for the sake of Heaven (Sha'ar Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh, derush 1; Sha'arei Kedusha 3:8).

notes_en.en: The Arizal explained (Sha'ar Ha-gilgulim, introduction 2): "Sometimes a person will perform some great mitzva through which he will merit that the soul (nefesh) of some righteous person from the early generations will be impregnated within him (mit'aber bo), and then it is possible that he will be rectified and refined to such an extent that the soul of this man returns to be at the level of the soul of that very righteous person…" "And everything depends on the value of the mitzvot that this person performs, for there are mitzvot that have in their special power the capacity to draw the nefesh of a righteous person in the secret of ibur (impregnation), and there are mitzvot that draw the ruaḥ of a righteous person…" He further explained that from this there is also a benefit for the righteous person whose spirit was impregnated in this man, for through this his legacy continues to bear fruit in the world.

sections.title_en: The Attitude toward Maggidim and Other Revelations
sections.body_en:
As stated, one of the kinds of revelation that a person may merit is through a 'maggid', which is created by virtue of his good deeds or his Torah study. One of the great figures who merited revelations of a maggid was Rabbi Yosef Karo: by virtue of the Mishna study to which he was accustomed, a maggid was created that revealed to him secrets of the Torah, and Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote these revelations down for himself in his own handwriting. About seventy years after his passing, they collected from these revelations that he had written for himself and printed them in a book called 'Maggid Meisharim'.

The Arizal explained (Sha'ar Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh, derush 1): "The matter of the angels who are revealed to a person and inform them of future events and secrets, and who are called 'maggidim' in the books – these are created from a person's engagement in Torah and mitzvot." "And the power of the angel made from engagement in Torah is greater than the power of the angel made through that mitzva." He further explained: "There are maggidim that are entirely truthful, and they are those made from Torah or mitzvot performed in their perfection; and there are maggidim that lie in some of their words, and there is in them an admixture of deceit and falsehood. And the reason is that if the person had some evil aspect, or something false, in that Torah or in that mitzva that he did, then the angel created from it is also composed of good and evil, and the good aspect in it speaks words of truth, and the evil in it speaks words of deceit." The Arizal further explained (ibid.): "There are people to whom the aforementioned maggidim are not revealed at all, and there are those to whom they are revealed, and everything is according to the aspect of their souls." That is to say, there are righteous people whose souls are suited to the revelation of maggidim, and then the maggidim are revealed to them; and indeed we find kabbalists and ḥasidim who wanted to receive maggidim who would reveal to them secrets of the Torah. And there are righteous people to whom maggidim are not revealed, because the matter does not suit their souls. Apparently, these righteous people merit to deepen and be precise in their understanding of the Torah, which is the greatest revelation (see the next halakha), and they do not wish to divert their minds and mix into their study revelations that require clarification and examination.

Rabbi Ḥayim of Volozhin testified that he heard from his teacher, the Gaon Rabbi Eliyahu of Vilna (in the introduction to Sifra De-tzni'uta), "that many times several maggidim from heaven came early to his door with their request and petition, wanting to transmit to him the secrets of the Torah without any toil. And he did not incline his ear to them at all. And one of the maggidim pressed him greatly. Despite all this, he did not look at its great appearance, and he answered and said to it: I do not want my attainment in His Torah, blessed be His Name, to be through any intermediary whatsoever. Only my eyes are lifted to Him, blessed be His Name: what He wishes to reveal to me and to give me as my portion in His Torah, blessed be His Name, through my toil with which I have toiled with all my strength, He, blessed be His Name, will give me wisdom; from His mouth knowledge and understanding; that He grant me an understanding heart, and my kidneys will become like two springs, and I will know that I have found favor in His eyes. And I want only that which is from within His mouth. And the attainments through the angels, the maggidim and the princes of the Torah, for which I have not toiled and in which I have not become wise – I have no desire for them." He further related that the Gaon of Vilna once sent him to his younger brother, who was great in Torah, "to tell him as a command in his name that he should not accept any maggid angel that would come to him, for in a short time a maggid angel would come to him." And he added that although "our master the 'Beit Yosef' (Rabbi Yosef Karo) had a maggid, that was two hundred years ago, when the generations were as they should be, and he dwelt on the holy soil. Not so now, when those who break through [the bounds] have multiplied, and especially outside the Land, it is entirely impossible that it be wholly holy of holies without any admixture at all. And especially revelations that are without Torah (that is, concerning future events and the like) – his soul loathed them. And they were not considered by him at all." However, revelations of the souls of righteous people were precious in his eyes (the fourth mode in the previous halakha). Also revelations that he merited during his sleep through the ascent of his soul were dear to him, but he did not consider them as primary, for they came without the toil of Torah.5

notes_en.en:
Rabbi Ḥayim of Volozhin testified (ibid.) that the Gaon of Vilna merited the ascent of his soul during his sleep at night, and that at times the souls of righteous people were revealed to him and revealed to him hidden matters of the Torah. However, he wrote: "What the soul attains, wondrous and awesome attainments, in sleep through the ascent of the soul… is not considered by him so much as a great principal thing; the principal thing is what a person attains in this world through toil and effort when he chooses the good… But what the soul attains in sleep, which is without effort and without choice and will, is only the receiving of reward, that the Holy One, blessed be He, gives a taste in this world of the World to Come." He further testified (ibid.) that the souls of righteous people, such as Yaakov Avinu and Eliyahu the prophet, were also revealed to him while awake, and the novel insights revealed to him through them were precious in his eyes. However, what he principally relied upon in understanding the hidden matters of the Torah was what he clarified through his toil in Torah.
The Gra further wrote (in his commentary on Mishlei 16:4) that every person has the possibility of receiving ruaḥ ha-kodesh from the roots of his soul, by which to know his own particular path; however, if he is not clean of sin and lusts, his spirit will mislead him to fall from heaven to earth without his being able to rise. Therefore we ought not to walk in great matters and in wonders, but to direct all our deeds to God, in fulfilling the positive commandments and being careful about the negative commandments, according to the Torah.

sections.title_en: The Hidden Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh in Torah Study
sections.body_en:
There are many levels of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, and what is common to all of them is that by virtue of a person's elevation in Torah and wisdom, in the refinement of his character traits and in good deeds, he merits supernal inspiration. Sometimes this is a revealed inspiration, such that the one who merits it is aware that he has received a divine illumination, and through it he understood an idea or merited to receive its formulation, or it granted him strength of spirit to perform great deeds for the sake of the whole of Israel.

And sometimes ruaḥ ha-kodesh rests in a hidden manner, that is, it grants inspiration with whose help a Torah scholar merits to understand the Torah and to be more precise in it, and to succeed in explaining many things through a single idea, and only after some time does it become clear that that understanding was inspired by ruaḥ ha-kodesh. Likewise, all the true explanations and novel insights (ḥiddushim) of the sages of Israel are by divine inspiration, akin to prophecy and ruaḥ ha-kodesh. As the Sages said (Bava Batra 12a): "From the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets… but from the sages it was not taken… and a sage is preferable to a prophet." The Ramban explained: "Although the prophecy of the prophets, which is vision and revelation, was taken, the prophecy of the sages – which is by way of wisdom – was not taken; rather, they know the truth through the ruaḥ ha-kodesh within them." And through this they attain with their intellect things that they would not attain by the intellect in the natural way (Ritva there). And although only rarely were the sages of Israel aware, at the time of their study, of the ruaḥ ha-kodesh stirring within them and helping them understand more than they could have understood according to their intellect, after some time, when their Torah teachings became settled and were included in the body of the Oral Torah, it became clear that their words were said through ruaḥ ha-kodesh. Apparently, good deeds performed with greatness out of pure intention, or especially good advice or especially deep consolation, are also through hidden ruaḥ ha-kodesh.6

notes_en.en:
In the book Toldot Adam by Rav Eliyahu Ba'al Shem of Chelm (5280-5343), chapter 9, s.v. "Hineh", he explained the two kinds of ruaḥ ha-kodesh: conscious and unconscious. In Yismaḥ Moshe (Toldot, s.v. "Ve-hineh") he explained that there are three levels in ruaḥ ha-kodesh: 1) complete awareness, in which ruaḥ ha-kodesh speaks from within his throat without his knowing anything of what it said before it spoke from his mouth; 2) ruaḥ ha-kodesh entered into his own words, and after he finished his words he sensed that he had spoken with its help; 3) he did not sense that ruaḥ ha-kodesh had assisted him. An example of awareness of ruaḥ ha-kodesh is the words of the Ra'avad in his glosses on the Rambam (Hilkhot Lulav 8:5): "Ruaḥ ha-kodesh has already appeared in our study hall…"; and there (Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 6:14): "Thus was it revealed to me from the secret of the Lord to those who fear Him." However, as brought above, all the words of Torah that the sages of Israel innovated and explained are considered [to have been said] through ruaḥ ha-kodesh.
And so wrote Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 6:50; 52), that everything that a seasoned student innovates properly is included in ruaḥ ha-kodesh. End quote. And this is ruaḥ ha-kodesh that is recognizable only after some time, after the words are accepted and become settled within the body of the words of Torah. Similarly, he explained in Pri Tzaddik (Ha'azinu 5) that the Written Torah is recognizably descending from heaven like rain, and the Oral Torah is like dew, whose descent from heaven is not noticeable; only when one sees that the ground is moist does one understand that dew has descended from above (and so too there, Ki Tetze 15). Rav Tzadok further wrote (Likutei Ma'amarim 11:10): "Ruaḥ ha-kodesh is the person's own speech, from his own side, only when it is with all his vitality – then it is ruaḥ ha-kodesh, a spirit from that supernal holiness, which is the wisdom of God, may He be blessed… That is, when his speech reaches the root of his vitality, and this is from the aspect of concealment… And the prophet was formerly called 'the seer' (ha-ro'eh), for he sees how it is the word of God, and the Shekhina speaks from within his throat…." He further explained that the root of prophecy is from Moshe Rabbeinu, and the root of ruaḥ ha-kodesh is from the attribute of David, through the awakening of understanding (bina) in the heart, from which come repentance and the wisdom of the Oral Torah (Takanat Ha-shavin 6:93). He further wrote (Yisrael Kedoshim 6:57-58) that the highest level a person can reach in this world is ruaḥ ha-kodesh, and sometimes even an ignoramus (am ha-aretz) can reach it through his connection to the root of his hold on the words of Torah, for in the future "they shall all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them" (Yirmeyahu 31:33), and this is through the holiness of the performance of the mitzvot.
On the advantage of a sage over a prophet, the Prisha wrote (ḤM 66:21) that a sage can sometimes change laws and rule against the halakha on the basis of assessment (umdana), and can also innovate laws through his analytical reasoning (pilpul), as Otniel ben Kenaz innovated, whereas a prophet cannot change [anything]. And see Ha'amek Davar, Bereshit 23:1, who explained the words of the Sages that Avraham was secondary to Sara in prophecy as referring to the attainment of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, for in prophecy he was greater than she. And the reason she was greater than he in ruaḥ ha-kodesh is that Avraham was occupied with leading people and could not seclude himself in his tent in holiness and purity as Sara could. End quote. From here there is a further explanation for the great figures who merited ruaḥ ha-kodesh in a hidden rather than a revealed manner: because they were occupied with leading the public and taught Torah to students, and did not seclude themselves.

sections.title_en: Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh out of Devotion to the People of Israel
sections.body_en:
There is a further manifestation of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, which empowers the one who merits it to perform great deeds to save individuals or the public. The Rambam explained (Guide for the Perplexed 2:45) that there are twelve levels of ruaḥ ha-kodesh and prophecy. The first level of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, from which one can ascend to the following levels, is the one that moves a person to perform great deeds, and all the judges who saved Israel merited it, as it is stated (Shoftim 2:18): "And when the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judge and saved them from the hand of their enemies." And as is stated concerning Yiftaḥ, who volunteered to save Israel from the hands of the children of Amon: "And the spirit of the Lord came upon Yiftaḥ" (Shoftim 11:29; Abarbanel there). And likewise it is stated concerning Shimshon (Shoftim 13:25): "And the spirit of the Lord began to move him," and thus he began to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines. And likewise it is stated concerning King Shaul, when he heard that the Ammonites had threatened to kill all the people of Yavesh Gil'ad, and would agree to let them live only if they consented that the Ammonites gouge out everyone's right eye as a sign of submission and disgrace: "And the spirit of God came mightily upon Shaul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (I Shmuel 11:6). And he gathered all Israel to war against the Ammonites and struck them, and saved the people of Yavesh Gil'ad. And likewise Queen Esther, when she was prepared to give up her life for the rescue of Israel, merited ruaḥ ha-kodesh, as it is stated (Esther 5:1): "Now it came to pass on the third day that Esther clothed herself in royalty, and stood in the inner court of the king's house, opposite the king's house"; the Sages said (Megilla 14b): "Esther clothed herself in royalty" – "that ruaḥ ha-kodesh clothed her." And even Moshe Rabbeinu, from the time he began to be concerned for Israel, merited ruaḥ ha-kodesh at this level, and by its power he struck the Egyptian, separated the quarreling men, and came to the aid of Yitro's daughters. And our teacher and master Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook ztz"l said that a spirit of courage of this kind rested upon the leaders of Israel when they decided on the 5th of Iyar 5708 to establish the State despite grave apprehensions (Or Li-netivati 45).

This quality is merited by people who are ready to give of themselves for the sake of others, as we learned from the officers (shotrim) of Israel in Egypt. After Moshe and Aharon came to Pharaoh and demanded in the name of God that he send Israel out, Pharaoh commanded the Egyptian taskmasters to make the labor heavier on Israel: until then they had been accustomed to supply them with straw for making the bricks, but from now on Israel would bring the straw themselves, and at the same time they were obligated to continue to produce the same quantity of bricks that they had been accustomed to produce. Pharaoh also appointed Israelite officers who would be responsible for enforcing the new order. "So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw. And the taskmasters pressed them, saying: Complete your work, each day's task in its day, as when there was straw. And the officers of the children of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten, saying: Why have you not completed your quota of making bricks both yesterday and today, as before?" (Shemot 5:12-14). The Sages said (Shemot Rabba 1:28) that over every ten Israelites one Israelite officer was appointed, and over every ten officers one Egyptian taskmaster was appointed. And when they did not manage to produce the quantity of bricks, the Egyptian taskmasters would beat the Israelite officers, so that they would beat the Israelites to make them exert themselves to fulfill Pharaoh's decree. But the officers absorbed the blows and did not beat the Israelites, for they had pity on them. In time, when God told Moshe to appoint seventy elders who would bear the burden of the people with him, Moshe said before God: "I do not know who is worthy and who is not worthy." God said to him (Bamidbar 11:16): "Whom you know to be the elders of the people and its officers, and take them to the Tent of Meeting, and let them stand there with you." The Sages said (Bamidbar Rabba 15:20): "Because they gave themselves over to be beaten for the community, therefore: 'And they shall bear the burden of the people with you' (Bamidbar 11:17). This teaches you that the Holy One, blessed be He, made them equal to Moshe. From here you learn that whoever gives himself over for Israel merits honor, greatness and ruaḥ ha-kodesh."

sections.title_en: Halakha Is Not Decided by Prophecy or Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh
sections.body_en:
The Sages said that halakha is not decided on the basis of prophecy, ruaḥ ha-kodesh or a bat kol, because after God gave the Torah to Israel through Moshe Rabbeinu, the sages of Israel must decide halakhic questions on the basis of their study of the Torah and not on the basis of knowledge they received from heaven. And so the Sages said (Temura 16a): "Three thousand halakhot were forgotten during the days of mourning for Moshe. They said to Yehoshua: Ask [God, through a prophet or the Urim Ve-tumim]. He said to them: 'It is not in heaven' (Devarim 30:12)." They turned to Pinḥas son of Elazar the priest, that he should seek a heavenly answer for the forgotten halakhot. He too answered: "It is not in heaven." They turned to his father, Elazar son of Aharon, who was then the High Priest. He answered: "A prophet is not permitted to innovate anything from now on"; rather, the sages of Israel must decide the halakha on the basis of their study of the Torah, as it is stated (Vayikra 27:34): "These are the commandments which the Lord commanded Moshe for the children of Israel at Mount Sinai," and since [it says] "These are the commandments" – "a prophet is not permitted to innovate anything from now on" (Megilla 2b). Indeed, the Sages said (Temura ibid.) that Otniel ben Kenaz, through his deep study and analytical reasoning (pilpul) in the Torah, succeeded in restoring and re-establishing one thousand seven hundred halakhot out of the halakhot that had been forgotten after the death of Moshe Rabbeinu. Similarly, the Sages said that after more than three hundred years, when Shmuel the prophet, the greatest of the prophets after Moshe Rabbeinu, arose for Israel, they turned to him with a request that he inquire through prophecy how one should act regarding the forgotten halakhot. He answered: "A prophet is not permitted to innovate anything from now on." And so all the prophets conducted themselves: while engaged in halakha, they did not avail themselves of prophecy but deliberated on the Torah according to their intellect, because prophecy is intended for guiding the people in matters of ethics and conduct, or for temporary directives (hora'ot sha'a), and not for deciding halakha.

Similarly it is related (Bava Metzia 59a-b) that the Sages disagreed about the law of 'the oven of Akhnai', which was an earthenware oven that had been cut into rings and reassembled, with a layer of sand placed between ring and ring, and on the outside a thin layer of plaster joining the rings. According to Rabbi Eliezer the vessel is considered broken and is not susceptible to ritual impurity, because the sand, which is not susceptible to impurity, separates the rings. And according to the Sages, since a layer of plaster joins the rings, the vessel is considered whole and is susceptible to impurity. The debate between them intensified, and none of Rabbi Eliezer's arguments were accepted. Rabbi Eliezer said to them: "If the halakha is in accordance with me – let this carob tree prove it. The carob tree was uprooted from its place a hundred cubits… They said to him: One does not bring proof from a carob tree. He then said to them: If the halakha is in accordance with me – let the water channel prove it. The water channel flowed backward. They said to him: One does not bring proof from a water channel. He then said to them: If the halakha is in accordance with me – let the walls of the study hall prove it. The walls of the study hall leaned to fall. Rabbi Yehoshua rebuked them, saying to them: If Torah scholars are defeating one another in halakha, what concern is it of yours? They did not fall, out of respect for Rabbi Yehoshua, and they did not straighten, out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer, and they still stand leaning. He then said to them: If the halakha is in accordance with me – let it be proven from heaven. A bat kol came forth and said: What do you have against Rabbi Eliezer? For the halakha is in accordance with him everywhere! Rabbi Yehoshua stood on his feet and said: 'It is not in heaven'… for the Torah was already given at Mount Sinai," in which it is stated (Shemot 23:2): "Incline after the majority." And so the Sages ruled, in halakha and in practice.

sections.title_en: One May Avail Oneself of Ruaḥ Ha-kodesh in Halakhic Rulings
sections.body_en:
Indeed, we find that in the decision to rule in accordance with Beit Hillel, they availed themselves of a bat kol, which is akin to prophecy. The Sages said (Eruvin 13b): "For three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagreed; these said the halakha is in accordance with us, and those said the halakha is in accordance with us. A bat kol came forth and said: These and those are the words of the living God, and the halakha is in accordance with Beit Hillel." The Sages asked about this: "Since these and those are the words of the living God, why did Beit Hillel merit to have the halakha established in accordance with them?" They answered: "Because they were agreeable and forbearing (humble), and they would teach their own words and the words of Beit Shammai, and moreover they would put the words of Beit Shammai before their own words."

Many explained that although halakha is not decided on the basis of heavenly revelations such as prophecy, ruaḥ ha-kodesh and a bat kol, one may avail oneself of them when, after all the halakhic deliberations, an evenly balanced doubt remains. For example, in the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, on the one hand Beit Hillel were more numerous, and on the other hand Beit Shammai were sharper (Yevamot 14a), and they availed themselves of a bat kol that said the halakha is in accordance with Beit Hillel (Tosafot, Yevamot 14a; Ḥida).

And some say that even in a situation of doubt it is forbidden to decide halakha on the basis of heavenly revelations. Even if there were a thousand prophets holding one view, and against them a thousand and one sages, one follows the majority and takes no account of the fact that they are prophets (Rambam's introduction to the Mishna). According to this view, in the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel too, the ruling in accordance with Beit Hillel was because they were the majority, as the Torah commanded (Shemot 23:2): "Incline after the majority." And the bat kol that came forth and proclaimed that the halakha is in accordance with Beit Hillel was intended to encourage them and strengthen them for having ruled correctly.7

notes_en.en:
The Tosafists (Yevamot 14a, s.v. "R. Yehoshua") asked: why did they take into account the bat kol that proclaimed that the halakha is in accordance with Beit Hillel (Eruvin 13b), whereas regarding the oven of Akhnai they decided that one does not take a bat kol into account (Bava Metzia 59b)? In their first answer they wrote that they did not take the bat kol into account regarding the oven of Akhnai because perhaps it came forth for the honor of Rabbi Eliezer and not because that is the halakha. In their second answer they wrote that they did not accept the bat kol regarding the oven of Akhnai because it was contrary to the rules of decision-making, for it was established in the Torah that one follows the majority. From both answers it emerges that had it been clear that the bat kol was said with regard to halakha and not contrary to the rules of decision-making, they would have taken it into account. Our master Rav Kook added and explained (Mishpat Kohen 92, pp. 174-175) that according to Tosafot one may indeed rely on a heavenly revelation when it comes of its own accord, but one may not inquire of heaven in order to decide halakha; therefore the doubts that arose after the passing of Moshe Rabbeinu were not resolved by turning to prophecy, ruaḥ ha-kodesh or the Urim Ve-tumim.
However, according to the Rambam (introduction to the Commentary on the Mishna), in any case halakha is not decided on the basis of heavenly revelations. Moreover, if a prophet comes and says that God commanded him in prophecy to say that the law is such-and-such, or that the halakha follows so-and-so – "he is a false prophet," and is liable to death by strangulation. Rather, the prophet may state his halakhic opinion as one of the sages, and not in the name of his prophecy (Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 9:4). And the ruling in accordance with Beit Hillel would have been so even without the bat kol, since they were the majority, and the bat kol only strengthened their words (Pri Ḥadash [?], Yesodei Ha-Torah 9:3). And so our master Rav Kook concluded, that the Rambam "completely locked the way of knowing the laws of the Torah from heaven by means of prophecy." However, there is still a difficulty from what we learned in Eruvin (6b), in the first possibility, that before the appearance of the bat kol one who wishes to act in accordance with Beit Shammai may do so, but after its appearance one may not. Perhaps one can say that after the appearance of the bat kol, in practice nearly all the sages were strengthened to decide according to what they held in their own minds, that the halakha is in accordance with Beit Hillel; thus in practice the halakha was decided by the sages and not by the bat kol.
According to the Ḥida (Shem Ha-gedolim, Ma'arekhet Ha-gedolim, yud, 224), it is possible that the Rambam too agrees that in a case of doubt which the sages are unable to decide by the power of their intellect, one may rule on the basis of a bat kol, except that any sage who, by his own reasoning, does not agree with the bat kol may disagree and rule otherwise. It follows that according to this view there is no dispute between the Rambam and Tosafot. Similarly the Meiri wrote (in the introduction to his commentary on Avot) that in matters where analogy and reasoning did not suffice, prophecy would sometimes clarify for them every mystery. And according to the Or Same'aḥ (Yesodei Ha-Torah 9:4), according to the Rambam one does not rule on the basis of a bat kol, but one does take it into account in establishing the stature of the sages; for example, that Beit Hillel are preferable to Beit Shammai since they were agreeable and humble, and therefore it is fitting to rule in accordance with them.
The Ḥida further wrote (ibid., and Birkei Yosef OḤ 32:4) that although one does not decide halakha on the basis of a bat kol, one may clarify the facts on its basis. And so wrote the Mishneh La-melekh (Hilkhot Ishut 9:6), in a case where the son of a Jewish woman became mixed up with the son of a maidservant, that one may clarify through prophecy which is the son of the Jewish woman. And so wrote Maharatz Ḥayot (Ḥullin 5a), and so it is implied by the Arukh La-ner (Rosh Hashana 21a). And in Yad Eliyahu of Ragoler (Pesakim 43), he inclined to agree with the ruling of a pious man who decided, on the basis of ruaḥ ha-kodesh, which was the kosher meat and which the tereifa in two pieces that had become mixed together. On the other hand, some hold that even a clarification of facts, if it bears on halakha, is not clarified on the basis of a bat kol or prophecy (Maharam Ḥaviv, Tosefet Yom Ha-kippurim 75a; Tosafot Yom Tov, Yevamot 16:6; Yad David, Eruvin 64b).

sections.body_en:
There are two main branches in the Torah. The first is matters of halakha, with which the authors of the Mishna and Gemara and those who continued them, the commentators and poskim in every generation, were occupied, clarifying the guidance of the Torah as practical halakha. The second is the spiritual contents of the inner dimension of the Torah, which are also called 'the secrets of the Torah' and 'words of Kabbala', with which the prophets, the masters of aggada, of [Jewish] thought, and the kabbalists were occupied. On the one hand, matters of the spirit are higher, and they are the soul of the Torah, and ruaḥ ha-kodesh stirs more openly in the great figures who engage in them. On the other hand, the authority of the rabbis who engage in the revealed part of the Torah to decide halakha is greater, since from the time the Torah was given, halakha is decided only according to the sages' understanding of the Torah, and not on the basis of heavenly revelations. Therefore, when there is a clash between a ruling according to halakha and a ruling written in the books of Kabbala, such as the Zohar and the books of the Arizal, one must rule according to halakha. And it is a kal va-ḥomer (an a fortiori argument): if even a prophet, whose prophecy is at a higher level, is forbidden to decide halakha on the basis of prophecy or ruaḥ ha-kodesh, all the more so one may not decide halakha on the basis of words of Kabbala, which were said at a lower level of ruaḥ ha-kodesh.

The Gra added and explained that there is no dispute between the Gemara and the Zohar, and all who claim that there is a dispute between them either did not understand the Gemara or did not understand the Zohar (Keter Rosh, Ma'amarim 15). And so it emerges from the words of the Zohar, that the Tanna'im and Amora'im arranged the Talmud according to the secrets of the Torah (Zohar Ḥadash [?], Ra'aya Meheimna, vol. 3, 244b). However, after all is said and done, if it appears to the poskim that in a certain law there is a clash between halakha and Kabbala, one must rule according to the rules of halakha, since the authority to decide is given to the sages according to the rules of the Talmud.

Indeed, in practice we have not found disputes between halakha and Kabbala; rather, at times guidance was stated in the words of Kabbala that is not brought in the Gemara and in the words of the poskim. In such cases the poskim wrote that one may act according to the Kabbala, but one may not obligate the public to do so, for from the words of Kabbala one may learn good practices but not establish halakhot. Therefore, for example, one cannot obligate the ḥazan to repeat and say "Hashem Eloheikhem emet" ("the Lord your God is true") at the end of Keriat Shema in order to complete 248 words in Keriat Shema (Responsa of Rav Eliyahu Mizraḥi 1). However, sometimes, with the encouragement of the sages, the public accepted a custom on the basis of Kabbala, as in the custom of the ḥazan to repeat and say "Hashem Eloheikhem emet", and since this became the practice, one must act this way by virtue of the custom.

Sometimes it is explained in the Zohar or in the writings of the kabbalists that the halakha follows one of the views mentioned in the words of the poskim. And although it is agreed that one may not decide halakha on the basis of heavenly revelations, many of the greatest rabbis, inspired by the words of the kabbalists, ruled in accordance with the halakhic view that matches the view of the kabbalists, especially in the laws of prayer and blessings. This was the view of Rabbi David ben Zimra, Rabbi Yosef Karo and the Ḥida. And some ruled according to the rules of decision-making and the accepted custom, contrary to the words of the kabbalists, and so ruled the Rema and the Rashal.8

notes_en.en:
Rabbi Eliyahu Mizraḥi (Responsa of the Re'em 1) wrote that when a practice appears in the Kabbala that was not mentioned in the Talmud and the poskim, one may not compel the public to act in accordance with it, even in a matter in which many have acted according to the Kabbala. The Radbaz (Responsa 4:36) added that where there is a dispute between halakha and Kabbala, one rules according to halakha. Many wrote their words as halakha, as complementing one another, among them the Knesset Ha-gedola (Kelalim be-darkhei ha-poskim 1-2), MA OḤ 25:20; MB 42; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 29. And the Ḥatam Sofer (OḤ 51) wrote: "Whoever mixes words of Kabbala with settled halakhot is liable for sowing kilayim (forbidden mixtures)," meaning that it is forbidden to mix reasoning based on Kabbala into the deciding of halakha (and so he ruled in OḤ 100 regarding shilu'aḥ ha-ken, sending away the mother bird).
However, after accepting the principle that one does not rule on the basis of heavenly revelations, many were accustomed to take the words of Kabbala into account when they do not clash with the words of halakha. As Rav Avraham Zacuto wrote in Sefer Yuḥasin (first ma'amar, entry on Rashbi), when the words of the Zohar do not disagree with the Gemara, the practice is to act according to the Zohar. This was cited in Responsa Maharival (5:41), and therefore he ruled according to the Zohar (3:146a) that even when the Levite is a Torah scholar and the Kohanim are ignoramuses, the Levite should wash their hands before Birkat Kohanim. Sefer Yuḥasin further wrote (ibid.) that when the poskim disagreed about a halakha and the Zohar decided in favor of one of the views, the practice is to rule in accordance with it. Therefore, in the dispute whether one answers Amen after the blessing 'Ga'al Yisrael' in Shaḥarit – according to the Rosh one answers, and according to the Rambam one does not answer – the practice is not to answer. And so wrote the BY and SA (OḤ 66:7), that the practice is not to answer, based on the Zohar (1:132b). And although the Rema there wrote that the practice is in accordance with the view of the Rosh, to answer, nowadays, even according to the custom of those of Ashkenazic descent, the ḥazan concludes the blessing quietly so as not to enter into the dispute whether to answer. Similarly regarding putting on tefillin on Ḥol Ha-mo'ed: according to the Rashba one does not put them on, and according to the Rosh one does. The Radbaz (4:8) and the SA (OḤ 31:2) decided, on the basis of the Kabbala, not to put them on. And in Responsa of the Rema of Fano 108, he even wrote: "If the Zohar disagrees with anyone who was among the commentators or the Ge'onim, as long as the language of the Gemara can bear it – everyone else is set aside in favor of the interpretation of the Zohar." On the other hand, the Rema wrote that the practice is to put on tefillin on Ḥol Ha-mo'ed, and so wrote Responsa Maharshal 98. And in Responsa of Rabbi Moshe Provençal (1:54) he explained that the practice was to put on tefillin on Ḥol Ha-mo'ed because custom and the decision of the poskim prevail over the words of the Zohar. Yet even in this, the custom of those of Ashkenazic descent in the Land of Israel is not to put on tefillin on Ḥol Ha-mo'ed, in accordance with the view of the kabbalists (see Peninei Halakha: Mo'adim 10, note 1).
Also when the Arizal decided in favor of one of the views on the basis of the Kabbala, many act in accordance with him, especially regarding prayer and blessings. For example, according to the Rambam and SA OḤ 46:8, the morning blessings (Birkhot Ha-shaḥar) are recited only over things from which the person benefits; therefore a lame person should not recite 'Ha-mekhin mitz'adei gaver' ("Who directs the steps of man"), and a blind person should not recite 'Poke'aḥ ivrim' ("Who opens the eyes of the blind"). Likewise one should not recite the blessing 'Ha-noten la-ya'ef ko'aḥ' ("Who gives strength to the weary") found in Ashkenazic siddurim, since this blessing is not mentioned in the Talmud. However, according to the Ge'onim all Israel should recite all the morning blessings, for they were instituted for the good of the whole world. And likewise one recites 'Ha-noten la-ya'ef ko'aḥ'. And the Ḥida wrote in Birkei Yosef 46:11-12 that the practice follows the Arizal, in accordance with the Ge'onim. And he added that had the BY seen the words of the Arizal, he would have agreed with him (see Peninei Halakha: Tefilla 9:3, note 1).
And it seems that even those who are accustomed to rule according to the Kabbala agree that it is forbidden to rule on the basis of heavenly revelations; rather, it is a known rule that in a time of need one may rule in accordance with one of the views even when the custom was in accordance with the other view, and if so, for those who act according to the Kabbala it is considered a need to act in accordance with the view that better suits the intentions of the Kabbala.
We find that sometimes one relies in halakhic rulings on the custom of Israel, which presumably took shape with the help of the ruaḥ ha-kodesh that is revealed in the whole of Israel. As we learned, when the Sages were in doubt how to carry the knives for the Pesaḥ offering on Shabbat, they looked to the custom of Israel and said that surely they acted according to the law, for "if they are not prophets, they are the sons of prophets" (Pesaḥim 66a). And so wrote the book Yad Eliyahu (Pesakim 25), that every custom accepted in Israel is considered to have been accepted through ruaḥ ha-kodesh. And they said in the name of the Ba'al Shem Tov that every book that has been accepted by Israel has ruaḥ ha-kodesh drawn into it (She'erit Yisrael, Sukkot, p. 117). And see Halakhot Ketanot 1:9.
